newsitem.title: USA: HUD chief warns U.S. near housing crisis for poor.
newsitem.headline: HUD chief warns U.S. near housing crisis for poor.

text.p: Outgoing U.S. housing secretary Henry Cisneros warned on Tuesday that the country is near a crisis in providing affordable housing and urged Congress to reverse a dangerous strategy on the issue.

"We are nearing a crisis that could force millions of American families and children to live in substandard housing and to live one paycheck away from homelessness," Cisneros said in his final major speech as secretary of Housing and Urban Development at the National Press Club audience.
Cisneros, who was dogged during his four-year tenure at HUD by questions over payments he had made to a former mistress, is scheduled to step down by January 20.
The HUD secretary said the Clinton Administration inherited the highest level of severe housing problems since the mid-1970s, and Congress has responded "in the worst way possible."

"Housing vouchers that help Americans afford housing, have been cut completely for three straight years now," said Cisneros, who became the first Hispanic mayor of a major U.S. city when elected Mayor of San Antonio, Texas in 1981. He remained in the post until 1989.
Cisneros also described promising efforts under his tenure to tackle homelessness, transform public housing and to turnaround inner city decay.

But Americans must continue to be concerned about the availability of jobs for welfare recipients, high levels of poverty and homelessness, and a growing cynicism that the U.S. can solve its toughest social problems, Cisneros said.
"We live in a time of too much cynicism," which corrodes the country's ability to implement even the smallest solutions, Cisneros said.

On homelessness, Cisneros said the Clinton Administration is successfully implementing the "Continuum of Care" approach to homeless assistance, including an increase of federal funds from $331 million to $931 million.
As a result, HUD serves up to 14 times more homeless persons than in 1992, he said.
The "Continuum" program allows providers to reach more mentally-ill homeless people.

Cisneros added that after decades of neglect, more than 23,000 of the worst public housing units have been replaced during Clinton's first term. Small scale, townhouse and garden-style housing is replacing mammoth apartment buildings, he said.
And residents are being connected with employment and educational opportunities, he said.
